title: Asia stocks rally as Korean chips surge and oil retreat lifts sentiment
full_text:
Investing.com -- Asian stocks extended a sharp global technology rebound on Tuesday, with South Korea and Japan leading regional gains as investors returned to beaten-down chipmakers following Wall Street’s biggest rally in about seven months.
A further retreat in oil prices, after U.S. President Donald Trump signalled that fresh strikes on Iran were unlikely if negotiations progressed, also lifted sentiment by easing inflation concerns, although uncertainty surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the looming U.S. inflation report kept investors cautious about the durability of the recovery.
The MSCI Asia Pacific index rose 2%, with South Korea’s KOSPI up 4.3%, Japan’s Nikkei gaining 2.8% and TOPIX advancing 2.2%.
Wall Street’s biggest rally in seven months lifted the S&P 500 2.4%, Nasdaq Composite 2.7%, Nasdaq 100 by 3.4%, Dow 2.15% and Philadelphia Semiconductor Index 6.9%. In Asian trade, Nasdaq 100 futures were unchanged, while S&P 500 futures edged up 0.1%.
Nvidia fell 4.2% amid a board probe into possible foreign targeting of CEO Jensen Huang. Reports alleged links to a Chinese businesswoman suspected of passing information to Beijing. The board said it saw no evidence of compromised company secrets. Nvidia reports earnings next week.
Korea, Taiwan and Japan lead the technology rebound
SK Hynix rose 6.3% and Samsung Electronics 4.9%. Kioxia gained 6.6%, TDK 5.2%, Murata 5.9% and LG Innotek 5.1%. Taiwan’s Taiex surged as much as 6.4%; TSMC rose 0.9%, Largan 5.6% and Foxconn 0.5%, while Sony fell 0.4%.
Taiwan’s seven-session slide, its longest since 2022, reversed after regulators cut short-selling limits to 3% of 30-day average volume from 30%, raised margin requirements to 130% from 90% and kept a NT$500 billion ($15.2 billion) stabilisation fund available.
Japan and Taiwan entered bear markets last week; Korea’s index was more than 40% below its summer peak and Taiwan’s 16% below its record. Samsung and SK Hynix had each lost more than 16%.
Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 ahead of a possible Tuesday IPO roadshow, seeking up to $69.3 billion. Its IPO and CoreWeave results will test AI investor appetite after hedge funds rapidly cut technology exposure.
Meanwhile, brent was $91.56, down 1% after a nearly 6% Monday slide to an early-September low. Trump said further strikes on Iran were unlikely if nuclear talks progressed after meeting Qatar’s prime minister.
China trade and regional data in focus
China’s October exports rose 35.2%, beating 33.5% forecasts but easing from September’s 36.3%. Imports jumped 41.6%, above 32% estimates.
The trade surplus topped $1 trillion for a second year, supported by AI shipments. China has been ASEAN’s largest trading partner since 2009, linking its trade momentum to regional supply chains.
Japan’s household spending plunged 6.8% year-on-year in September, against a 3.1% decline forecast and marking its steepest drop since 2020. However, weak consumption complicates the BOJ’s outlook, with markets expecting a December 18 rate hike from the current 1.25%.
The NZX 50 gained 1%. Labour led National in preliminary party votes, 29.36% to 29.21%, but National won 42 seats against Labour’s 36. National, ACT and New Zealand First together hold 67 of 131 seats; around 400,000 special votes remain, with final results due November 27.
The ASX 200 rose 1.1%, Singapore’s STI gained 1.6%, while India's Nifty-50 futures traded flat.
October U.S. CPI is due Tuesday, with headline and core prices forecast to rise 0.3% and 0.2%. Fed hike odds climbed to 84% from 74% a week earlier following strong jobs data.

title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia CEO Huang over Chinese scandal
full_text:
Investing.com-- U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI was investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy for Beijing.
Speaking to reporters during a press briefing at the White House, Trump said “I know the FBI is looking into (Huang) and I think that he’ll be in good shape.”
“I asked him that question. Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said I had no idea that she was a spy and I really believe him,” Trump said.
Trump’s comments come amid a rapidly escalating controversy over Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of a Singapore-based client of Nvidia, who U.S. authorities reportedly concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Huang admitted to the affair in a memo released earlier this week, and said that he will cooperate with any investigation into the matter.
Nvidia shares slid over 4% on Monday after its board said it was initiating an investigation into the matter, although they found no reason to believe U.S. national security or Nvidia’s confidential information was compromised.
Separately, the scandal was seen attracting Congressional scrutiny. House of Representatives Democrat leader Hakeem Jefferies said on Monday that Congress needed more answers regarding the Nvidia situation.
Democrat Senator Chris Coons called for an investigation into Huang and Nvidia to "determine whether our national security was compromised."
"We need answers about the relationship between AI billionaires and the Trump administration, who’s making these decisions, and who’s really got their hand on the wheel," Coons said in a social media statement.
Trump was seen forming a close relationship with Huang over the past two years, having repeatedly lauded the Nvidia CEO for his contributions to the American economy, while also taking him along for several high-profile state visits-- most notably Trump’s Beijing trip earlier this year.
Nvidia and Huang are also facing a proposed class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing the CEO’s ties with a suspected Chinese spy.
Huang sits at the heart of one of America’s most valuable companies, largely due to its status as the maker of the most advanced artificial intelligence chips available in the market.
China has been a long-standing point of contention for Nvidia, after the U.S. effectively blocked most of its advanced chip sales to the country since 2022. Huang has repeatedly called for allowing more chip sales to China, albeit to mixed results from Washington.
A key point of concern in the ongoing scandal is the governance implication, given that Huang is a key figure in Nvidia with few potential successors.
But analysts said it appeared unlikely, for now, that the scandal would result in Huang stepping down. The Nvidia CEO has led the company since co-founding it in 1993.

title: China trade balance shrinks more than expected in Oct; imports surge
full_text:
Investing.com-- China’s trade surplus shrank more than expected in October, pressured by strength in the yuan, while growth in both exports and imports surpassed market expectations.
China’s trade balance shrank to a surplus of $105.28 billion in October, government data showed on Tuesday. The print was lower than expectations of $126.50 billion and fell from the $133.53 billion surplus seen in September.

The softer balance was in part driven by recent strength in the yuan, which hit an over four-year high in October, following a series of strong midpoint fixings by the People’s Bank.
A stronger yuan tends to weigh on the value of overseas sales.
Surging imports also weighed on China’s trade balance, amid growing domestic demand for materials tied to the artificial intelligence buildout.
Semiconductors and data center components were the biggest drivers of import growth.
Imports grew 41.6% in October against expectations of 32%. Growth also accelerated sharply from 31% seen in the prior month.
China’s commodity imports were seen improving, especially those of oil. Crude imports grew 13.1% month-on-month to 41.9 million tonnes in October, reaching their highest level since March.
Copper imports fell 2.2% month-on-month, while iron ore fell 3.8%.
Growth in Chinese exports surpassed expectations in October, with exports rising 35.2% year-on-year against expectations of 33.5%.
Overseas demand for electronic components, raw materials– chiefly rare earths and metals– and electric vehicles remained strong, underpinning export growth.

title: Analysis-Market rout tests BOJ’s upbeat view of financial conditions
full_text:
By Leika Kihara
TOKYO, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The recent volatile swings in global markets are putting greater attention on the Bank of Japan’s assessment of financial conditions, a key component of its policy framework that could sway the pace and timing of interest rate increases.
With markets returning to some measure of calm after a steep selloff in AI stocks, many analysts expect the BOJ to keep raising interest rates, with the next hike projected to come as soon as December.
But the recent rout has tested the central bank’s view that brisk AI demand will underpin the economy, with the wealth effect from booming stock prices giving households and companies more spending power.
It has also put the spotlight on the BOJ’s financial conditions language, which serves as a key gauge of how close its policy rate is to levels deemed neutral to the economy, thus offering clues on the pace and timing of rate rises.
While the BOJ’s escalating warning over inflation risks has preoccupied market participants, the less discussed guidance on financial conditions may increase in prominence if the AI market rout keeps equity prices on a downtrend, some analysts say.
"The BOJ’s basic view is that financial conditions remain loose, which won’t immediately change just because stock prices are falling," said former BOJ official Tetsuya Inoue, who is now executive economist at Sony Financial Group.
"But if asset prices remain unstable, it may hurt growth by cooling corporate mood and spending from households with stock holdings. Depending on market moves, it could give the BOJ reason to put off a rate hike in December."
STOCK WEALTH EFFECT
The BOJ has stressed the need to continue raising interest rates to counter upside price risks and prevent underlying inflation from overshooting its 2% target.
It has also justified rate hikes by saying financial conditions are loose, pointing to low real borrowing costs, strong corporate funding demand and rising bank lending.
While describing interest rates and funding indicators as key measurements, the BOJ said it also looks at asset prices in gauging financial conditions since stock prices and exchange rates affect household and corporate spending.
"For example, the uptrend in stock prices likely contributed to a decline in firms’ cost of capital and helped support private consumption through wealth effects," the BOJ said in its quarterly outlook report released last month.
Such a positive cycle might go into reverse if the stock market adjustment persists and hits Japan’s once risk-averse households, who have recently piled into stocks to ride the AI boom.
Japanese households’ stock holdings reached 486 trillion yen ($3.08 trillion) in June, BOJ data showed, up 47% from year-earlier levels, accounting for 19.3% of their total wealth.
"The stock wealth effect is small compared with the US, but could have a sizeable impact on consumption as many in the younger generation now hold stocks," said Seisaku Kameda, the BOJ’s former top economist, who is an economist at Japan’s Sompo Institute Plus.
At last month’s policy meeting, the BOJ said financial conditions remained accommodative "in light of recent developments in asset markets," as well as data showing still-low real rates and funding costs.
But a summary of opinions from the October meeting, released on Tuesday, exposed a rift in how board members viewed the prevailing financial conditions, with some seeing little impact of past rate hikes, while others warned of the potential hit to growth.
In a sign of the board’s increased attention, one member called for assessing financial conditions using three measurements: the real interest rate gap, corporate finance and the bank lending channel, and asset prices.
"Asset prices, in particular, are affected not only by monetary policy but other factors," as seen in rising stock prices driven by AI-related demand, the member said.
For now, markets will be on the lookout for how Governor Kazuo Ueda will describe the impact of the market rout on financial conditions in a speech due on November 30, which precedes the BOJ’s next policy meeting on December 17 and 18.
"Theoretically, if stock prices fall, that would tighten financial conditions," a source familiar with the BOJ’s thinking said, a view echoed by another source. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly.
"There’s still some time before the December meeting," a third source said. "Nobody knows how markets would be behaving then."

title: Exclusive-Anthropic’s nearly $70 billion IPO plan briefly circulated to banks, then retracted
full_text:
By Echo Wang
Nov 9 (Reuters) - Details of Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO, including plans by the AI company to raise nearly $70 billion, were briefly circulated to banks before being retracted late on Monday, according to emails seen by Reuters.
A representative of Anthropic sent a copy of a securities filing that showed it aimed to sell about 867 million shares at a price range of $70 to $80 per share, then followed up with an email saying details about the pricing were inaccurate. Anthropic said in the second email it would update the filing later.
Anthropic declined to comment. The email did not specify to bankers what was erroneous, and Reuters was unable to determine what was incorrect.
The original email whose details were retracted showed Anthropic planned to sell 866.7 million Class A shares, including a secondary offering. Anthropic itself would sell about 843.3 million shares, while existing shareholders would sell an additional 23.3 million shares. The IPO would raise $69.3 billion at the top of the range.
Separately, the original filing showed that Anthropic had lined up $26 billion in investments from some of the world’s biggest technology companies alongside its IPO, underscoring the increasingly intertwined financial ties underpinning the AI boom.
Alphabet’s Google, Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Micron Technology, Microsoft and TSMC had agreed to participate in the private placement of Anthropic’s Class N common stock at the IPO price, which would close immediately after the IPO, the original filing showed.
Anthropic is expected to formally launch the roadshow on Tuesday, with pricing expected in the following week.
The Anthropic IPO comes at a time when other companies in the AI infrastructure and data center sectors have delayed or withdrawn their planned listings, facing a rise in interest rates that has helped fuel a punishing selloff in shares and bonds of AI operators such as CoreWeave Inc and broader questions about the sustainability of AI spending.
Investors had previously discussed a valuation of as much as $2 trillion for Anthropic, but expectations have since come down, with the $1.5 trillion figure viewed as the high end of the range, Reuters previously reported.
Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives including Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, who is now Anthropic’s president, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models.
The company’s rapid growth has been underpinned by Google and Amazon, which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors.
Anthropic had nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Google, underscoring how its rapid growth depends on vast amounts of future capacity, some of it reliant on financing beyond the company’s control.
Anthropic’s quarterly growth rate has declined sharply even though revenue stood at almost $17 billion for the three months ended September 30, the company revealed in an amended filing earlier in the month.

title: Billionaire tax measure on California ballot defeated
full_text:
By Ann Saphir and Peter Henderson
SAN FRANSISCO, Nov 9 (Reuters) - A billionaire tax that US Senator Bernie Sanders and other progressives championed as an antidote to economic inequality and a potential model for the rest of the country was defeated in California, US media projected on Monday.
Proponents had estimated Prop 40 would raise $100 billion in revenue, most of which would have been earmarked for healthcare programs to offset federal funding cuts designed to pay for tax breaks enacted last year under President Donald Trump’s "One Big Beautiful Bill." Those tax breaks, largely benefiting wealthy individuals and corporate interests, passed with Republican-only support in the US Senate.
The failure of the billionaire tax marks a blow to the left wing of the Democratic Party, even as Democrats won decisive majorities in both houses of Congress in a sweeping midterm election rebuke of Trump and his policies.
Supporters of Prop 40, which targeted stocks, bonds and business assets rather than earned income, reasoned it stood a healthy chance of enactment in a state where voter rolls favor Democrats over Republicans by a nearly two-to-one margin.
But California Governor Gavin Newsom, a likely candidate for the Democratic Party presidential nomination in 2028, came out against the measure, arguing that Prop 40 would backfire in the long run by creating an unwelcome climate for upwardly mobile high-tech entrepreneurs.
His opposition and division among party leaders led initial support for the measure to wane ahead of the vote.
Opponents argued the tax would prompt the ultrawealthy to leave the state, taking their income-tax payments and job-producing enterprises with them, and discourage entrepreneurs from building their startups in California in the first place.
Labor unions were also divided. Billionaires chipped in more than a quarter of a billion dollars that helped fund ads that framed the measure as a gateway to more aggressive taxation for all Californians and as a threat to their retirement accounts.
Those arguments may have resonated at a time when the pinch of higher gas prices and affordability concerns have put a broad swathe of the country in a sour economic mood.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin and at least 11 other billionaires contributed a collective $269 million to a political action committee called Building a Better California, which in turn poured more than $300 million into campaigns opposing Prop 40.
Incoming Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden has signaled, however, that taxing the ultrawealthy remains a central goal for the Democratic Party as a whole.
“The committee will redouble its efforts to ensure billionaires pay their fair share and hold tax cheats accountable,” he said in a November 4 statement outlining the panel’s priorities.

title: Honda raises full-year profit outlook, books $3 billion in EV-linked costs in Q2
full_text:
By Daniel Leussink
TOKYO, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Honda Motor on Tuesday raised its annual outlook by 20%, underpinned by robust US hybrid demand and a weak yen, even after it booked another $3 billion in charges to restructure its electric-vehicle business.
The quarterly results, like Toyota Motor’s last week, highlight how Japanese automakers are becoming more dependent on the US market, where demand for hybrids - not EVs - is growing and where they face no competition from Chinese rivals.
Honda’s additional writedown on the EV business comes after it booked more than $9 billion in charges in the previous financial year, which pushed Japan’s second-largest automaker into its first annual loss in nearly 70 years.
The company had made considerable progress in talks with suppliers over settling the restructuring costs, Chief Financial Officer Masao Kawaguchi said.
"We want to settle everything, as much as possible, within this financial year," Kawaguchi said, adding that Honda wanted to resolve the issue as early as possible.
The total toll of more than $12 billion is among the biggest hits from an EV restructuring by any legacy automaker.
Honda kept its estimate for EV restructuring costs this financial year at 520 billion yen ($3.29 billion), including the 484.8 billion yen booked in the latest quarter.
The company raised its full-year operating profit forecast to 780 billion yen from 650 billion yen.
Operating profit for the July-to-September quarter fell 39% from a year earlier to 118 billion yen, well below the 250 billion yen median forecast in a poll of nine analysts by LSEG.
It is betting heavily on hybrid vehicles, particularly in the US, where sales rose 9% in the second quarter and accounted for half of its global retail sales of 823,000 vehicles.
LOWER GLOBAL SALES FORECAST
Honda also cut its full-year global vehicle sales forecast by 7% to 3.16 million, due mainly to falling sales in China.
It said it expected slightly tougher conditions in North America in the second half, partly due to higher interest rates and incentives.
On Monday, Honda said it would build a $3 billion auto plant in Ohio that will be able to produce 240,000 hybrid cars a year and start production in 2029.
Global automakers have recently posted weaker results, with Volkswagen reporting a steep quarterly loss after a writedown on its stake in Porsche as well as weakness in China, while Hyundai Motor cut its annual outlook due to soft demand and rising raw material costs.
Toyota bucked the downtrend by raising its full-year profit forecast as strong hybrid sales boosted earnings.

title: Porsche SE swings to €2.8 billion nine-month loss on Volkswagen impairment
full_text:
Investing.com -- Porsche SE, the holding company that controls Volkswagen, swung to a loss of €2.8 billion after tax in the first nine months of 2026, from a profit of €1.2 billion a year earlier, mainly because of a non-cash impairment on the carrying amount of its Volkswagen stake. The company said persistently difficult conditions in the car industry are putting pressure on its core investments.
Its adjusted group result after tax, which strips out items such as the impairment, fell about 42% to €930 million from €1.59 billion. The result from accounting for Volkswagen on an equity basis fell to €0.8 billion from €1.7 billion, while the contribution from its 25% stake in Porsche AG rose to €0.2 billion from €0.1 billion.
Group net debt was €5.1 billion, almost unchanged from the end of 2025.
"The Volkswagen Group’s quarterly results clearly show that the agreed measures to strengthen competitiveness, reduce costs and sustainably improve profitability must be implemented swiftly," Chairman Hans Dieter Pötsch said. "It is now the management’s task and responsibility to deliver."
The portfolio of smaller investments was a bright spot. Its after-tax result rose to €135 million from €13 million, helped by a revaluation of its stake in Quantum Systems, and its carrying amount rose to €669 million from €535 million. Porsche SE acquired a stake in the U.S. space company Stoke Space Technologies in the quarter, with an investment in the low double-digit millions of dollars.
Porsche SE also won a legal case. Germany’s Federal Court of Justice dismissed appeals by 40 plaintiffs, mostly U.S. hedge funds, who sought €5.4 billion plus interest over Porsche SE’s earlier build-up of its Volkswagen stake. The ruling is final, and the related lawsuits are to be dismissed.
For 2026, Porsche SE expects an adjusted group result after tax of between negative €0.5 billion and positive €1.5 billion, and net debt of €4.7 billion to €5.2 billion. The forecast depends on the Volkswagen and Porsche AG outlooks, which assume current tariffs persist and exclude any effect from the Middle East conflicts.

full_text:
Investing.com -- Austrian paper and packaging company Mayr-Melnhof Karton shares jumped more than 16% Tuesday after the Austrian company announced it would sell a 70% stake in its packaging business to U.S. private equity firm KPS Capital Partners in a deal valuing the business at €2.4 billion ($2.69 billion), including debt.

MM Group expects to receive cash proceeds of €1.8 billion to €1.9 billion from the transaction. The company plans to use the funds to repay debt, pursue strategic opportunities, and return €500 million to €600 million to shareholders.
The company’s stake in the packaging business could fall to 20% if certain 2027 earnings targets are not met, with no additional payments to MM Group.
MM Packaging operates more than 50 production sites across 19 countries and employs approximately 8,500 people. The business manufactures consumer packaging products, including folding cartons, labels and leaflets, for the food and beverage, pharmaceutical and healthcare, beauty and personal care, and household care sectors.
The deal, which has been approved by MM Group’s supervisory board, is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory and other approvals. For the French business, the acquisition is subject to consultation processes with workers representatives.

title: Honda raises full-year outlook despite second-quarter profit slump
full_text:
Investing.com -- Honda Motor (TYO:7267) raised its full-year profit forecasts on Tuesday as stronger motorcycle sales and demand for hybrid vehicles in North America helped offset a sharp earnings hit from restructuring its electric-vehicle business.
Net profit attributable fell 42.8% to ¥65.8 billion in the three months ended September 30, while operating profit dropped 39% to ¥118 billion, missing the ¥250 billion median estimate in an LSEG poll of nine analysts cited by Reuters.
For the six months ended September 30, net profit attributable rose 65.7% to ¥516.8 billion, although it fell short of analysts’ estimate of ¥643.2 billion. Revenue increased 13.2% to ¥12.04 trillion, while operating profit climbed 48.1% to ¥648.7 billion.
Honda booked ¥484.8 billion in costs related to restructuring its electric-vehicle business during the second quarter. Excluding these charges, first-half adjusted operating profit rose 71.3% to ¥1.13 trillion.
Motorcycle sales provided the strongest support, with first-half volumes increasing 10.6% to a record 11.9 million units, driven by growth in India and Brazil.
Automotive sales, however, fell 6.6% to 1.57 million vehicles, reflecting weaker demand in China. Higher North American sales of compact cars and hybrids helped offset the decline.
Honda raised its full-year operating profit forecast by 20% to ¥780 billion from ¥650 billion, while lifting its net profit forecast by 25% to ¥500 billion from ¥400 billion. It also raised its revenue outlook to ¥24.4 trillion from ¥24.15 trillion, citing stronger motorcycle sales, higher North American vehicle volumes and favourable currency movements.
The company maintained its annual dividend forecast at ¥70 per share. It also raised its motorcycle sales outlook to 23.3 million units from 22.8 million, while cutting its automobile sales forecast to 3.16 million from 3.39 million.

title: Vodafone raises profit, cash flow guidance despite €3.6 billion H1 loss
full_text:
Investing.com -- Vodafone raised its full-year profit and cash flow guidance Tuesday, even as the telecom group reported a €3.6 billion loss for the first half because of non-cash charges. It now expects fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDAaL, a measure of operating profit after lease costs, of €13.2 billion to €13.4 billion, up from €13.0 billion to €13.3 billion.
Adjusted free cash flow is now seen at €2.8 billion to €3.0 billion, up from €2.6 billion to €2.9 billion.
At the midpoints, the new ranges imply organic growth of about 7% in adjusted EBITDAaL and 21% in adjusted free cash flow. Vodafone said that was the first year of a plan for double-digit organic cash flow growth.
First-half revenue rose 11.4% to €21.9 billion, helped by consolidating Safaricom, VodafoneThree and Telekom Romania, partly offset by currency moves. Service revenue rose 12.8% to €18.4 billion, or 5.8% on an organic basis, with growth in all segments.
Adjusted EBITDAaL rose 12.6% to €6.5 billion, or 6.4% organically, with the margin up 0.5 percentage point to 29.5%.
The reported loss compares with a €1.1 billion profit a year earlier. It reflects an impairment in Germany tied to higher interest rates and a write-down of deferred tax assets in the U.K. after Vodafone bought out CK Hutchison’s stake in VodafoneThree, partly offset by a non-cash gain on the Safaricom deal.
The interim dividend rose 2.5% to 2.306 euro cents a share.
Africa led growth, with organic service revenue up 13.4%. Vodafone Business grew 5.8%, with a best-ever 6.6% in the second quarter. Germany, the biggest drag, grew just 0.4%, and the U.K. 0.9%. “Germany is not yet where it needs to be,” Chief Executive Margherita Della Valle said, adding that an action plan is under way.
Vodafone has delivered more than €200 million of gross cost savings and about 3,000 role reductions across Europe and shared operations in the half. It has separately announced 2,300 more job cuts in Germany. It also raised its VodafoneThree synergy target to £0.8 billion a year by fiscal 2030 and £1 billion by 2032.
A legal challenge in Kenya remains over Vodacom’s purchase of a further 20% of Safaricom, after the High Court declared the deal void in September. The Court of Appeal has ordered the status quo kept while it hears the case.

title: U.S. inflation data ahead; Huang scandal fallout - what’s moving markets
full_text:
Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock indices hover around both sides of the flatline, as investors await key inflation figures and assess fragile sentiment around the artificial intelligence trade. Oil falls to roughly $90 a barrel on hopes for a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war, while Nvidia shares tick higher in after-hours trading following a selloff on Monday triggered by a scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang.
1. Futures mixed
U.S. stock futures pointed to a mixed open on Tuesday. By 03:17 ET (08:17 GMT), the S&P 500 futures contract had risen by 13 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq 100 futures had dipped by 22 points, or 0.1%. The Dow futures contract was higher by 252 points, or 0.5%.
The main averages on Wall Street gained in the prior session, as a renewed bout of dip-buying powered the benchmark S&P 500 to its best day since April. Optimism once again brightened around AI following last week’s roller-coaster moves in stocks exposed to the nascent technology, with a tracker of the semiconductor industry in particular notching its largest one-day gain since July.
Following a series of selloffs and recoveries, the S&P 500 is now down "only" 0.25% in the four business days after the U.S. midterm elections, analysts at Deutsche Bank noted. Traders have been attempting to gauge whether a major victory for Democrats, especially in gubernatorial races in states that host massive data center projects, will lead to a slowdown in AI development.
"There wasn’t an obvious catalyst for the bounceback, but as our equity strategists noted, equity positioning had become sizably underweight after last week’s moves, and in tech, positioning was now beneath its lows after Liberation Day," the Deutsche Bank analysts said.
2. CPI ahead
Attention now turns to the release of monthly U.S. inflation figures. Headline consumer prices are tipped to have risen 0.3% month-over-month in October. The annualized rate will not be released because a federal government shutdown last year prevented the collection of the consumer-price index for October 2025.
The so-called "core" gauge, which strips out volatile items like food and fuel, is seen increasing by 0.2% month-over-month.
Energy is still the "principal swing factor" for overall price gains, flagged analysts at Truflation, an alternative data provider. For October, Truflation has projected a 20.7% rise in energy prices versus a year earlier, with gasoline climbing 37.7%.
Higher costs at the gas pump partially fueled discontentment over affordability that helped drive a sharp rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump’s economic policy in midterm elections. American voters widely supported Democratic challengers to Trump’s Republican candidates in several statewide races, giving Democrats control over both chambers of Congress in the process. The victory could make it more difficult for Trump to aggressively pursue his policy goals, including the ongoing war with Iran and tariffs on global trading partners.
Crucially, the outcome of the Labor Department’s consumer-price index could sway projections for Federal Reserve interest rates. Solid labor market data last Friday may have given Fed officials more headroom to raise rates next month, after policymakers rolled out their first increase in three years in September. In theory, lifting borrowing costs can quell inflation, albeit at the risk of weighing on overall economic activity and the job market.
3. Oil slips to around $90
Also bolstering stocks has been a downward slide in oil prices, which has dragged the benchmark Brent crude futures contract to roughly $90 a barrel. As recently as late October, Brent was exchanging hands at over $115 a barrel, as markets fretted over the prospect of new and intense U.S. attacks on Iran in the wake of the midterms.
However, diplomatic efforts have appeared to gain momentum. Trump has signaled that he would like to find an end to the war with Iran, a conflict now in its ninth month that has been partly responsible for pushing up energy prices and elevating inflation.
The president’s comments came after a meeting with the prime minister of Qatar, a frequent mediator between Washington and Tehran. Still, Trump warned that U.S. is "locked and loaded," while describing Iran’s military as "effectively over." Citing an official familiar with the matter, Bloomberg News reported that talks between the U.S. and Iran will carry on and there will likely not be a fresh military escalation.
4. Nvidia shares in focus amid Huang scandal
Elsewhere, shares of Nvidia edged higher in extended hours trading after the AI-darling fell by more than 4% following the company’s announcement of an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang.
In a memo to employees, Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman from a Singapore-based firm who was allegedly a spy for China. The news has rattled Nvidia, who has become a bellwether -- and frequent financial backstop -- of the AI industry under Huang.
Speaking to reporters during a press briefing at the White House, Trump said “I know the FBI is looking into [Huang] and I think that he’ll be in good shape.”
“I asked him that question. Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said I had no idea that she was a spy and I really believe him,” Trump said.
5. Anthropic’s roughly $70 billion IPO plan retracted after circulated to banks - Reuters
Anthropic may begin formally marketing its potential blockbuster initial public offering on Tuesday, giving the Claude-maker the opportunity to pitch itself as a solid investment despite broader ructions in the AI sector.
The company reportedly sent bankers details of the IPO before retracting the pricing information, saying the figures were inaccurate, Reuters reported on Monday, citing emails seen by the news agency.
Anthropic initially circulated a copy of an IPO filing indicating plans to offer about 867 million shares at a price range of $70 to $80 apiece, potentially raising as much as $69.3 billion. But it later sent another email to bankers saying the pricing details were inaccurate and that an updated filing would be provided later, according to the Reuters report.

title: Microsoft pushes Trump to halt Chinese data center component ban: Reuters
full_text:
Investing.com -- Microsoft has been lobbying the Trump administration to abandon plans to bar imports of Chinese optical transceivers, a key component in AI data centers, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing three people familiar with the matter.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is working on the ban, which the administration has been weighing since at least August, the report said. Optical transceivers let data travel over fiber-optic cables inside data centers, and officials worry Beijing could use them to steal data, install malware or disrupt service.
Reuters reported that Microsoft is one of several companies and trade groups arguing that a ban could damage the U.S. edge over China in AI by further slowing data center construction. Microsoft has 35 data centers under construction in the U.S. and 134 planned, the report said, citing Cleanview data.
The company was among a handful of firms that met with White House science and national security officials in September to flag supply-chain risks, two sources told Reuters.
John Miller, general counsel of the Information Technology Industry Council, a tech lobbying group, told Reuters a ban "really threatens to arguably grind (the data center rollout) to a halt." He said many cloud companies have already bought the AI chips for their buildouts, and without transceivers to connect them, the chips "could just sit there waiting around unutilized."
Some data centers need millions of the devices to connect servers, routers and switches, Reuters said.
U.S. alternatives are limited. China holds two-thirds of the global market, according to Counterpoint Research, with Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight, which is on the Pentagon’s list of Chinese military-backed companies, dominating supply.
U.S. companies Coherent and Lumentum make competing technology but lack the scale to replace Chinese vendors, Reuters said, citing a report by the Foundation for American Innovation.
The report also said two of its sources confirmed the FCC is considering a threshold of 3.2 terabits per second. Such transceivers aren’t expected to ramp up until 2028, with widespread installation in 2029, which would give U.S. makers time to expand while avoiding friction with U.S. companies and Beijing.

BENGALURU, Nov 10 (Reuters) - REUTERS POLL- US FEDERAL RESERVE WILL HIKE FED FUNDS RATE IN DECEMBER TO 4.00%-4.25%, SAID ALL 101 ECONOMISTSREUTERS POLL-FED FUNDS RATE WILL PEAK AT 4.00%-4.25% IN CURRENT HIKING CAMPAIGN, SAID 56 OF 101 ECONOMISTSREUTERS POLL-RISK TO MEDIUM TERM US INFLATION VIEW HASN’T CHANGED SINCE MIDTERM ELECTIONS, SAID 29 OF 37 ECONOMISTSThe US Federal Reserve will hike interest rates for a second and final time in the current cycle in December, according to a majority of economists polled by Reuters who said the risks to their inflation outlook had not changed since the midterm elections.
Voters focused on the rising cost of living, fueled by Republican President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs and higher energy costs from the war with Iran, handed solid majorities in both houses of Congress to the Democratic Party.
However, the political shift is unlikely to bring rapid relief from inflation, even after oil futures tumbled more than 22% from their late-October high on hopes of a resolution to the nearly 9-month-old Middle East conflict.
A strong jobs market, resilient economic growth and inflation stuck above the Fed’s 2% target for nearly six years all suggest further tightening is required.
The central bank raised the federal funds rate in September but paused in October. It is forecast to hike one more time by 25 basis points in December to a 4.00%-4.25% range, unchanged from last month’s survey, according to all 101 economists in the November 6-10 Reuters poll.
"The Fed is at the mercy of incoming inflation data and it will lend itself to the Fed raising rates once more," said Tom Porcelli, chief economist at Wells Fargo. "There was a fair argument that the Fed could have easily raised rates at this October meeting."
Around 55% of forecasters, 56 of 101, expect December’s move to mark the end of the current cycle, also broadly steady compared with last month.
A strong minority, 45, including more than half of the primary dealers surveyed, still see at least two more increases ahead, in line with market pricing.
If the consensus view proves correct, just two rate rises would be the shortest Fed rate-hiking campaign in more than a decade.
A majority of economists who answered an additional question, 29 of 37, also said the risk to their medium-term inflation views had not changed since last week’s midterm elections.
There are differences of opinion among policymakers on the severity of the inflation threat.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday that the Fed should raise rates in December even if inflation cools and consider a bigger move if it accelerates, while a day earlier Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin said monetary policy should be moved only "with care."
The October Consumer Price Index, due later on Tuesday, is expected to show inflation picking up, a separate Reuters survey showed.
"I don’t think any softening in inflation is in the pipeline, to be honest. For me, the scenario is still of a meaningful re-acceleration in core inflation into the fall of the winter and Q1 of next year," said Jan Groen, chief US economist at Societe Generale.
The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, will remain more than a percentage point above 2% over coming quarters and not return to target until at least 2028, poll medians showed.
It is expected to average 3.5% and 2.6% this year and next, respectively, slightly higher than forecast last month.
The economy is expected to grow 2.2% this quarter after expanding at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, powered largely by AI-driven investment. On an annual basis, growth is forecast at 2.4% this year and 2.2% in 2027, slight upgrades from last month’s forecasts.

title: Reaction roundup: Experts, analysts weigh in on October CPI report
full_text:
Investing.com -- Wall Street’s focus on Tuesday was on the October U.S. consumer inflation report which came in hotter-than-expected. The data, combined with hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller, led to traders all but locking in an expected quarter-point rate hike in December and even considering a supersized half-point increase.
As per the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, headline CPI ticked up 0.4% M/M in October after a 0.6% rise in September. Economists had expected an increase of 0.3%. Core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, remained steady at 0.3% M/M, coming in higher than the anticipated 0.2% figure.
There were no Y/Y figures published in the CPI data on account of a U.S. government shutdown in October 2025.
The CPI also comes just days after a blockbuster nonfarm payrolls report. The combination of a strong labor market and persistent inflation sets the stage for monetary policy tightening, with the question now being just how big the rate hike will be next month.
While a 25 basis point increase is widely anticipated, the probability of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) delivering a 50 basis point rate hike has ticked up to nearly 11% from no odds before the CPI data, according to the CME FedWatch tool.
Waller earlier at an event in London said he would support a 25bps rate hike in December even if October inflation improves, and that a larger 50 bps move should be considered if price pressures stay strong.
Focus will now turn to the producer price index (PPI) later this week, followed by the latest reading on the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge - the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index later this month.
Wall Street opened lower after the CPI and Waller’s remarks, with the benchmark S&P 500 last down 0.7%. Interest-rate sensitive assets saw big reactions, with U.S. Treasury yields soaring as bonds were dumped and the dollar strengthening. The 2-year yield jumped 20.1 basis points to 4.748%, while the U.S. dollar index advanced 0.7%.

See below for various reactions to the CPI data:
Kevin Gordon, head of macro research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research:
“October CPI disappointed at both the headline and core levels, with clear impacts showing up from the increase in fuel prices.
Governor Chris Waller’s speech before the inflation report now reads quite timely, given his mention of core CPI increasing by 0.3% M/M (which did in fact happen in October) as a clear sign to—at the very least—hike in December and—in a more aggressive scenario—consider a 50bps rate hike at the next meeting.
While it’s likely early days for a 50bps rate hike discussion, the point is that inflation data are trending in the wrong direction as the labor market continues to strengthen by several metrics (most notably, the significant beat for October payrolls). We will wait for PCE signals that come from PPI later this week, but at this point, the data are stacking in favor of a coming hike.”
Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics:
“There's no silver lining to this U.S. CPI report…Following Waller's speech, a 50bp hike will now clearly be under consideration in December, though (for what it's worth) I think most FOMC members will stick to a more gradual approach.”
Justin Wolfers, professor of public policy and economics at the University of Michigan:
“Ugh. Latest inflation numbers just came out, and it's still running hot, and hotter than most expected. One hopes inflation starts returning to normal, but that's a hope right now, not a reality.
Today's numbers are CPI inflation. The Fed targets PCE inflation. And core PCE inflation is actually running a bit hotter than core CPI.”
Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management:
“Given the higher-than-desired inflation, it is even more likely now that the Fed will raise rates in December and although some are calling for a 0.5% increase in the Fed Funds target rate, we expect that they will only raise rates by 0.25% next month.
However, the new question is whether or not the Fed will follow that up immediately with a second 0.25% rate hike in January – which would have been unexpected before today – or whether they will take their time and raise rates for slowly next year (e.g. skip one or two meetings between rate hikes in 2027).
All of this matters for markets, because a more patient Fed would be easier for stock bulls to navigate, while a more aggressive Fed could prove to be too big of a headwind for the market to overcome next year.”
Robin Brooks, senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution:
“All the details of this CPI report are discouraging, but October was also the peak of the second big oil price shock this year and that's obviously going to bleed into core CPI inflation. So today's CPI reading is more backward-looking than normal.”
Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial:
“Not all current inflation pressures should be attributed to the war in the Middle East, although some are likely the result of supply constraints. Rather, part of today’s inflation is demand-driven. The Fed will take this into account and will likely raise rates in December to cool the demand side of inflation. One encouraging sign is that rent inflation has remained between 2.7% and 2.9% for the past 10 months.”
Peter Schiff, chief economist and global strategist at Euro Pacific Asset Management:
“The CPI will likely rise 5% in 2026 and by more than 7% in 2027, higher than any calendar year under Biden. The Fed's planned rate hikes are too little, too late to prevent this. The federal funds rate must be raised by at least 200 basis points now to possibly stop this train.”

title: Vanishing vessels and missing sailors: The Iran war’s human cost at sea
full_text:
By Maha El Dahan, Praveen Paramasivam and Mohammed Atti
DINDIGUL, India/DUBAI/BASRA, Nov 10 (Reuters) - V. Pandiselvi, the mother of Indian sailor Naveen Kumar, has not heard from her son for more than six months yet she still clings to hope he will return, crying as she replays old voice notes.
Kumar was one of six crew members assigned to work on two Iran-linked cargo vessels last seen in Iranian waters in May before disappearing. The vessels’ fate is still unclear.
Commercial ships have come under fire since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28. Tehran attacked ships to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz and the US in turn struck Iran-linked ships to impose a blockade on Iranian ports.
The UN’s International Maritime Organization has confirmed 130 "incidents" – mainly attacks – in the region since the conflict began, with at least 25 seafarers killed.
"We cannot bear this pain," Pandiselvi, 45, told Reuters from her one-bedroom house in the city of Dindigul in southern India’s Tamil Nadu state, struggling to keep her composure.
"You don’t need anyone to tell you what a parent would go through if they were to lose their child. We appeal to everyone involved to please come forward and help us."
Reuters spoke to shipping sources, Iraqi officials and the families of missing sailors in Iraq’s Basra and India’s Tamil Nadu state to reveal the human cost of Hormuz attacks.
The 23-year-old Kumar’s family took on considerable debt for him to complete a marine course and pursue his dream of working as a sailor, after which he left for a six-month crew contract he was told was based in Dubai. A week in, he found himself in Iran, to the consternation of his family.
’EVERY MINUTE IS AGONY’
Even before war broke out three months later, Kumar’s family was desperately trying to repatriate him. Then came radio silence.
"My mental condition had deteriorated into madness, I sent desperate messages," Pandiselvi said, adding she was sending him voice notes without any replies to a number she had saved as "Naveen Mariner" with an anchor emoji.
The family keeps the line active in hope their son picks up. A neighbour described her as listening to messages over and over, in tears.
"A terrifying question mark hangs over his fate: Is he still on that ship, or has something terrible happened to him? It’s causing a lot of confusion. Every passing minute is agony," Pandiselvi said.
Kumar had been deployed to the vessels Bridge 1 and Bridge 2, which disappeared around May 9. The two ships were not on the IMO’s list of incidents.
Iraq said in May it was monitoring the disappearance of the two vessels, which flew the Bolivian flag. No distress signals were received. Gulf ports requested information after communications with the crew were lost.
Khaled Saad al-Thaalibi, who heads the Iraqi maritime foundation in Basra, told Reuters the latest available information indicated the vessels’ Automatic Identification System (AIS) transmitted their last known position approximately 8 nautical miles from Iran’s Kish Island on May 9 at 4:50 p.m.
"We called the agent in Iran but he told us that he knew nothing about the incident and on the following day the Iranian search and rescue tried to look for the vessels but they found nothing," Thaalibi told Reuters from his office in Basra.
"We don’t know if the vessels sunk or were confiscated by a country."
The other Bridge 1 and 2 crew members missing are three Iraqis, one Pakistani and another Indian.
Sources familiar with the matter said the vessels were involved in Iranian trade and carrying steel.
NO ANSWERS
Haider Rahman al-Mayahi, a 22-year-old Iraqi sailor, was on the crew, his brother Youssef Rahman said.
"He left behind a one-year-old daughter and a father who suffered a stroke from the grief of his disappearance," he told Reuters, breaking down in tears.
Al-Mayahi’s family travelled to Iran seeking answers. They located the vessels’ owner, whom they identified only as an Iranian who told them he had no information on the vessels.
The family received conflicting theories about the vessels. Some shipping sources said they may have been struck by the US and sunk immediately while others speculated the crew had been detained by a Gulf state or Iran.
The Iranian agent who hired the Iraqi sailors did not respond to phone calls from Reuters.
Kumar’s family took out around 1.5 million Indian rupees ($16,000) in loans for him to complete his maritime training course and is now struggling with the financial burden.
They contacted the local agency that hired Kumar, Mumbai-based firm Lascar Marine, initially receiving assurances he would return soon. People from the agency later told the family they had no information. After that, calls went unanswered, the family said.
The agency did not reply to repeated calls from Reuters.
An order dated May 22, published on a government website, showed India’s Seamen’s Employment Office withdrew the recruitment license of Lascar Marine Services and barred its past and present directors from maritime business for five years, citing repeated failures to repatriate seafarers — including Kumar — or pay their wages.
The director of Seamen’s Employment Office did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Crew working aboard ships are usually contracted by agents like Lascar Marine and hired on six-month contracts. Since the Iran war, costs of hiring sailors have tripled with many working just one journey as risks mount.
One Dubai-based shipper told Reuters a crew member may make what they used to make in seven months in only two and then opt to go home. A captain, the highest paid crew member on a vessel, could make around $8,000 to $13,000 a month before the conflict. Now they can earn three times that.
"They ask for three months’ pay per month but after seeing what a journey entails they sometimes quit after one trip," the shipper said.
For Pandiselvi, Kumar’s mother, the allure of good pay is now meaningless.
"We worked tirelessly to secure our children’s careers and future," she said. "Now, seeing everything that has happened, we are left wondering what our lives have come to."

By David Shepardson
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - US traffic deaths fell in the first half of this year to the lowest rate since 2014, the government said on Tuesday, retreating from a spike during the 2020 COVID pandemic and several years in which road deaths remained elevated.
This year is on pace to be the fifth straight year of declines, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which said traffic deaths dropped 2.5% to 16,750 in the first half of the year. It was the lowest number since 2015 and down from 17,175 in the same period last year.
The fatality rate fell to 1.02 fatalities per 100 million vehicle miles traveled and the number of deaths fell to the lowest number since 2015.
Full-year traffic deaths for 2025 fell to the lowest number since 2019 and the fatality rate fell to 1.10 fatalities per 100 million vehicle miles traveled, the second-lowest yearly figure in US history, NHTSA said.
Deaths fell 5% in the first three months of 2026 but just 0.2% in the second three months.
One area of concern remains bicyclist deaths, which rose 4% to 1,148 last year. In 2023, bicyclist deaths hit their highest figure in more than four decades.
US traffic deaths jumped 10.8% in 2021 to 43,230, the most in a single year since 2005.
As US roads became less crowded during the pandemic, some motorists perceived police as less likely to issue tickets, experts said, resulting in riskier driving. Some drivers were also more likely to drive while being impaired by alcohol or drugs consumed at home during the pandemic.
The US fatality rate rose much higher than for other developed nations during the pandemic.
A 2023 NHTSA study found crashes directly cost taxpayers $30 billion, and society as a whole $340 billion. When quality-of-life valuations were included, the total cost to society ran to $1.37 trillion.

title: Brazil plans measures for 2027 fiscal savings, source says
full_text:
SAO PAULO, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Brazil will unveil in the next few days measures to achieve a fiscal adjustment equivalent to 0.5% of gross domestic product in 2027, a government source said on Tuesday.
The step comes after Brazilian financial markets sold off on the back of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s reelection late in October, as investors questioned the prospects for a fiscal adjustment sufficient to stabilize public debt.
Among the measures in the new fiscal plan is the exclusion of extraordinary revenue from the basis for calculating the constitutional spending floors for health and education even when there is a surplus, the source said.
Another pillar of the fiscal adjustment, which would amount to between 70 billion reais and 80 billion reais ($12.5 billion to $14.3 billion) next year, could be a new cut to tax benefits, according to the source.
A bill with the measures is set to be presented by a government-backed lawmaker, rather than directly by the government, the source added. The finance ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Local news outlet G1 first reported the government’s plan for a fiscal adjustment bill.
In a televised address to Brazilians on Sunday, Lula reaffirmed his commitment to fiscal responsibility and said he wanted to help bring down high interest rates.
The central bank paused an easing cycle last week, keeping the benchmark interest rate Selic at 13.75% as it grappled with a worsening inflation outlook that some analysts say has been boosted by market fears over a declining fiscal policy scenario.
Brazil’s real has weakened, long-term interest rates have risen and the benchmark Bovespa stock index has slumped after Lula’s election victory on October 25, when he defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a surprise runoff turnaround.
Gross public debt has risen more than 10 percentage points during Lula’s current term to reach 82.9% of GDP, amplifying concerns that campaign pledges would fuel additional government spending.

title: Goldman, Citi join global banks in $270 million stablecoin venture - Bloomberg
full_text:
Investing.com -- A consortium of global lenders including Goldman Sachs Group Inc (NYSE:GS), Citigroup Inc (NYSE:C), Banco Santander (NYSE:SAN), and Deutsche Bank (NYSE:DB) has committed approximately $270 million to fund a joint stablecoin venture, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The capital commitment is designed to finance the first five years of operations for the planned U.S.-incorporated issuer, which is currently operating under the internal codename Project Faro.
The injection formalizes an ambitious initiative detailed in September by 21 international institutions seeking to counter crypto-native incumbents through institutional-grade digital settlement assets. Participants are currently conducting an executive search for a chief executive officer to steer the entity toward a targeted commercial rollout in the first half of 2027.
While the venture initially aims to issue a dollar-pegged token, the consortium plans to subsequently expand issuance into other G7 currencies, prioritizing a euro offering. The product is intended to serve wholesale, institutional, and retail markets, streamlining cross-border transactions and digital asset settlements under established regulatory frameworks, including the U.S. GENIUS Act and Europe’s MiCA.
The collective push underscores a broader strategic effort among incumbent financial institutions to pool liquidity, operational infrastructure, and client distribution against sector leaders Tether and Circle. Established issuers currently dominate the roughly $290 billion stablecoin landscape, with Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC controlling about 85% of total circulation.
Regulatory tailwinds have increasingly catalyzed traditional finance’s push into digital assets, supported by federal legislation enacted in 2025 to create a defined legal perimeter for reserve-backed payment tokens. U.S. policymakers have frequently emphasized dollar-denominated tokens as critical instruments to reinforce the greenback’s global dominance while sustaining institutional demand for short-term Treasury debt.
Project Faro builds on exploratory work initiated in late 2025 by a founding group of 10 lenders seeking reserve-backed solutions on public distributed ledgers. The consortium has since broadened its geographic footprint to span North America, Europe, East Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, drawing participation from institutions such as Bank of America, UBS, Fidelity Investments, and Wells Fargo.
